title: Restoring Semantic Fidelity for Training-Free High-Resolution Image Generation in Diffusion Transformers

paper.title: Restoring Semantic Fidelity for Training-Free High-Resolution Image Generation in Diffusion Transformers
paper.abstract: Abstract. Diffusion Transformer (DiT)-based text-to-image models have recently achieved remarkable success in image synthesis. However, when directly applied beyond their training resolution, these models often suffer from severe semantic degradation, where meaningful semantic content disappears. Although existing training-free high-resolution generation methods can mitigate this issue, the inherent semantic degradation at high resolutions remains largely unresolved, leading to degraded fine-grained details. Furthermore, widely used structural guidance methods lack modeling of the structure and details in the intermediate trajectory, which degrades the quality of the generated results. In this paper, we propose a training-free framework for high-resolution image generation to address these challenges. First, we propose a text–visual scale-decoupled attention (TVSDA) module, which restores the model’s ability to generate semantically meaningful content at high resolutions by preserving the global receptive field of text tokens while aligning the receptive field of image tokens with the training resolution. Second, we propose a structure–detail guidance (SDG) strategy that explicitly models structural information and fine details through scale-wise and temporal-wise guidance, overcoming the limitations of conventional low-resolution guidance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly improves both structural coherence and detail fidelity over existing training-free DiT-based high-resolution generation approaches. The code is available at https://github.com/ljjcoder/Restoring-Semantic-Fidelity .

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: In recent years, text-to-image generation models ( Labs, 2024 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) based on Diffusion Transformers (DiT) ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) have substantially advanced image synthesis with remarkable visual quality. However, when the target resolution exceeds the training resolution, these models often fail dramatically ( Du et al., 2024b ; Bu et al., 2025 ) : meaningful semantic content disappears, and the generated images may collapse into semantically unrecognizable patterns, as shown in Figure 1 . This phenomenon, which we refer to as semantic degradation , has become a major obstacle for high-resolution generation scenarios. Figure 1. Illustrations of semantic degradation. When performing high-resolution inference with FLUX ( Labs, 2024 ) (trained at 1024 × \times 1024 and tested at 4096 × \times 4096), semantic structures completely disappear. Zoom in for better visualization. A straightforward solution is to further fine-tune pre-trained models on high-resolution images ( Guo et al., 2024 ; Hoogeboom et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Ren et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) . However, this strategy is often impractical due to the high computational cost and the limited availability of large-scale high-resolution training data. As a result, training-free high-resolution generation has attracted increasing attention ( He et al., 2024 ; Du et al., 2024a ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Bar-Tal et al., 2023 ; Lee et al., 2023 ; Du et al., 2024b ; Bu et al., 2025 ) . Early approaches were mainly developed for U-Net architectures ( He et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2024 ) , and are not readily applicable to DiT-based models. More recent studies ( Du et al., 2024b ; Bu et al., 2025 ) have begun to explore training-free high-resolution inference for DiTs, significantly improving generation quality. Despite recent progress, existing methods ( Du et al., 2024b ; Bu et al., 2025 ) primarily rely on low-resolution structural guidance, introducing structural priors during high-resolution inference rather than directly addressing the model’s intrinsic semantic degradation. If the model lacks the ability to generate semantically consistent content, such external guidance alone is insufficient to produce fine-grained details, as shown in Figure 2 . To address this issue, we propose a text-visual scale-decoupled attention (TVSDA) module to alleviate the model’s intrinsic semantic degradation at high resolutions. The core idea is to align the attention scale at high resolutions with that used during training. Concretely, attention for text tokens, which lack explicit positional information, is computed in a global manner, whereas attention for visual tokens with explicit positional information is confined within the training resolution. However, restoring semantic fidelity alone is not sufficient. Although TVSDA enables the model to generate semantically meaningful content, the resulting images often suffer from disorganized global layouts, manifested as repetitive local structures (see Figure 3 ). A natural next step is therefore to introduce a coarse structural prior, as in existing methods ( Du et al., 2024a ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Qiu et al., 2024 ; Bu et al., 2025 ) , to improve the global layout. Nevertheless, it still leaves two important residual failures (see Figure 5 ): (1) local semantic repetition, and (2) blurred fine details. These observations suggest that the remaining errors are no longer caused simply by a missing initial structure, but by a mismatch in how the reverse flow trajectory evolves at high resolution. This leads to the important question of our work: how should the high-resolution flow trajectory be corrected once semantic fidelity has been restored and a coarse structure has been initialized? To answer this, we perform an empirical analysis of the single-step predicted clean images across both different resolutions and different denoising timesteps (see Figure 6 ). We observe that lower-resolution predictions tend to provide more stable global semantic layouts, whereas higher-resolution predictions contain richer high-frequency details. Moreover, as denoising proceeds, later predictions become progressively sharper and reveal increasingly clear fine details. These observations suggest that structural coherence and fine-detail restoration should be guided in two ways: across scales and across timesteps. Based on this analysis, we propose a structure–detail guidance (SDG) strategy to refine the velocity field throughout inference. SDG consists of two key components. The first is Cross-Scale Guidance (CSG), which encourages the low-frequency components of the current high-resolution prediction to align with the structurally stable low-resolution prediction, while preserving the high-frequency components from the high-resolution branch. The second is Cross-Temporal Guidance (CTG), which leverages the progressive emergence of high-frequency details along the denoising trajectory to further sharpen fine structures. Ultimately, as shown in Figure 2 , with the integration of TVSDA and SDG, our method not only preserves coherent semantic layouts but also significantly enhances fine-grained details compared to previous methods. Figure 2. Visual comparison at 4096 × \times 4096 resolution. DiT-based methods I-Max ( Du et al., 2024b ) and HiFlow ( Bu et al., 2025 ) suffer from blurry backgrounds and a lack of high-frequency details, whereas our method restores fine-grained structures and produces sharper results. Zoom in for better visualization. The contributions of this paper are summarized as follows. • We propose a text–visual scale-decoupled attention (TVSDA) module to restore semantic fidelity by preserving global text interactions while constraining visual attention to training local regions. • We show that conventional low-resolution structural guidance is a natural but insufficient remedy: although it improves coarse layout, it still leaves local semantic repetition and blurred details. To address these residual failures, we analyze predicted clean images across scales and timesteps, and derive a structure–detail guidance strategy consisting of Cross-Scale Guidance (CSG) and Cross-Temporal Guidance (CTG) to refine the high-resolution flow trajectory. • Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms prior training-free DiT-based approaches in both generation quality and inference efficiency on high-resolution image generation tasks.

sections.heading: 2.1. Text-to-Image Generation
sections.text: Diffusion models ( Blattmann et al., 2023 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Song et al., 2020 ) have emerged as the prevailing framework for text-to-image generation ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Podell et al., 2023 ) , owing to their strong capability in modeling complex high-dimensional distributions. Early works ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Ho and Salimans, 2022 ; Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) performed denoising at the pixel level, resulting in significantly high computational costs during both training and inference. The Latent Diffusion Model (LDM) ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) was subsequently introduced to mitigate these costs, enabling more efficient training and inference while enhancing the model’s ability to generate high-resolution images. Despite these advances, the training resolution of current diffusion models remains well below that required for many real-world applications. When the target resolution exceeds the training resolution, generation quality deteriorates substantially. Fine-tuning with high-resolution images ( Ren et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) can address this issue, but it is computationally expensive and limited by the availability of high-resolution data.

sections.heading: 2.2. Training-Free High-Resolution Image Generation
sections.text: To address these issues, several works ( He et al., 2024 ; Du et al., 2024a ; Lee et al., 2023 ; Du et al., 2024b ; Bu et al., 2025 ) explore strategies to leverage pre-trained U-Net-based models (e.g., SDXL ( Podell et al., 2023 ) ) for high-resolution image generation without additional training. These methods can be broadly categorized into three types: (1) patch-wise methods ( Bar-Tal et al., 2023 ; Lee et al., 2023 ) , which divide the input into overlapping patches, perform standard denoising on each patch, and then fuse the results; (2) model component optimization methods ( He et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Jin et al., 2023 ) , which adapt selected components of the pre-trained model—such as self-attention layers ( Jin et al., 2023 ) or convolutional layers with dilated convolutions ( He et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2024 ) —for high-resolution generation; and (3) structural guidance methods ( Du et al., 2024a ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Qiu et al., 2024 ) , which leverage low-resolution images to provide semantic guidance for high-resolution generation. Recently, transformer-based diffusion models ( Labs, 2024 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) have significantly outperformed U-Net–based architectures. Consequently, several training-free high-resolution generation methods ( Du et al., 2024b ; Bu et al., 2025 ; Koh et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ; Yu et al., 2026 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) built on the transformer architecture have been proposed, which improve generation quality. However, these methods still tend to produce blurry results. In this work, we focus on high-resolution image generation using the transformer architecture. Unlike previous approaches, our method enhances generation quality by combining two strategies: restoring the model’s generative capabilities and refining the reverse denoising trajectory with structural and detail guidance.

sections.heading: 3. Background
sections.text: Before introducing our method, we briefly review the pretrained model, including its training and inference strategies as well as its architecture.

sections.heading: 3.2. Architecture
sections.text: Unlike previous U-Net-based models ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Podell et al., 2023 ) , modern generative models ( Labs, 2024 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) adopt the more expressive Multimodal Diffusion Transformer (MMDiT) ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) . The MMDiT architecture consists of modules such as FFN, adaLN-Zero blocks, and joint self-attention. Among these, only the self-attention module is resolution-dependent; the other modules operate on a per-token basis and are therefore resolution-agnostic. Therefore, we next describe in detail the joint self-attention mechanism for text and visual tokens. Let Q v Q_{\mathrm{v}} ( Q t Q_{\mathrm{t}} ), K v K_{\mathrm{v}} ( K t K_{\mathrm{t}} ), and V v V_{\mathrm{v}} ( V t V_{\mathrm{t}} ) denote the query, key, and value matrices of image and text tokens, respectively. In standard self-attention, image and text tokens share the same keys and values: (5) K = [ K t ; K v ] , V = [ V t ; V v ] , K=\left[K_{\mathrm{t}};K_{\mathrm{v}}\right],\qquad V=\left[V_{\mathrm{t}};V_{\mathrm{v}}\right], where [ ⋅ ; ⋅ ] [\,\cdot\,;\cdot\,] denotes concatenation along the token dimension. sections.heading: 4. Method
sections.text: As illustrated in Figure 1 , when the target resolution exceeds the training resolution, the pretrained model often produces images that lack meaningful semantic content. To address this limitation, we introduce a text–visual scale-decoupled attention module and a structure–detail guidance strategy. The former reformulates the self-attention mechanism to restore the model’s ability to generate meaningful semantic content, whereas the latter leverages cross-scale and cross-temporal guidance to maintain structural coherence while enhancing high-frequency details. An overview of the framework is illustrated in Figure 4 . Figure 3. Comparison of high-resolution generation results (DI: direct inference). Zoom in for better visualization. Figure 4. Pipeline of our method. During the DiT denoising process, Text-Visual Scale-Decoupled Attention (TVSDA) replaces the original attention to restore semantic generation capability, while Structure–Detail Guidance (SDG) preserves global structure and restores high-frequency details.

sections.heading: 4.1. Text-Visual Scale-Decoupled Attention
sections.text: In the joint self-attention layer, as the resolution increases, the receptive field of each query token grows quadratically ( Jin et al., 2023 ) , making attention overly uniform at high resolutions, causing it to attend to many irrelevant regions, and ultimately leading to semantic degradation. To mitigate this issue, we aim to align attention computation with the training resolution during high-resolution generation. For a visual query token q v i q_{\mathrm{v}}^{i} , which is associated with an explicit spatial position, it is natural to constrain its receptive field to the local region centered on itself, with a scale consistent with the training resolution. In contrast, a text query token q t i q_{\mathrm{t}}^{i} , lacking explicit positional priors, is not constrained in the same way. Motivated by this, we propose a text-visual scale-decoupled attention mechanism (TVSDA), which decouples attention scales for text and visual tokens. Specifically, attention is computed as follows: (1) Text queries q t i q_{\mathrm{t}}^{i} follow standard global attention (Equation 6 ), using the full set of keys and values. (2) Visual queries q v i q_{\mathrm{v}}^{i} use the full text keys K t K_{\mathrm{t}} and values V t V_{\mathrm{t}} , while the visual keys and values are restricted to a local neighborhood centered at q v i q_{\mathrm{v}}^{i} : (7) K ~ v i = K v ​ [ 𝒩 ⁡ ( i , s ) ] , V ~ v i = V v ​ [ 𝒩 ⁡ ( i , s ) ] , \tilde{K}_{\mathrm{v}}^{i}=K_{\mathrm{v}}[\mathcal{N}(i,s)],\quad\tilde{V}_{\mathrm{v}}^{i}=V_{\mathrm{v}}[\mathcal{N}(i,s)], where 𝒩 ⁡ ( i , s ) \mathcal{N}(i,s) denotes the set of visual tokens within a neighborhood of training scale s s around q v i q_{\mathrm{v}}^{i} . The visual attention output for q v i q_{\mathrm{v}}^{i} is defined as (8) Attn ⁡ ( q v i ) = softmax ⁡ ( q v i ​ [ K t ; K ~ v i ] ⊤ d ) ​ [ V t ; V ~ v i ] . \mathrm{Attn}(q_{\mathrm{v}}^{i})=\mathrm{softmax}\left(\frac{q_{\mathrm{v}}^{i}[\,K_{\mathrm{t}};\tilde{K}_{\mathrm{v}}^{i}\,]^{\top}}{\sqrt{d}}\right)[\,V_{\mathrm{t}};\tilde{V}_{\mathrm{v}}^{i}\,]. As shown in Figure 3 (b), TVSDA significantly restores the model’s ability to generate semantic content; however, the overall layout exhibits severe repetitive patterns.

sections.heading: 4.2. Initial Structural Guidance
sections.text: To preserve a reasonable semantic layout in high-resolution images, an effective approach is to introduce low-resolution structural guidance ( Du et al., 2024a ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Qiu et al., 2024 ; Bu et al., 2025 ) . This strategy incorporates low-resolution structural priors at the initial stage of the denoising process, and is referred to as Initial Structural Guidance (ISG). Specifically, given a generated low-resolution image x 0 L x_{0}^{L} , we upsample it to obtain x 0 , u ​ p H = upsample ​ ( x 0 L ) x_{0,up}^{H}=\texttt{upsample}(x_{0}^{L}) . We then inject noise at an intermediate timestep τ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \tau\in(0,1) : (9) x τ H = τ ​ x 1 H + ( 1 − τ ) ​ x 0 , u ​ p H , x_{\tau}^{H}=\tau x_{1}^{H}+(1-\tau)x_{0,up}^{H}, where x 1 H x_{1}^{H} denotes Gaussian noise. The value of τ \tau follows the setting in ( Bu et al., 2025 ) due to its strong empirical performance. The resulting x τ H x_{\tau}^{H} serves as the starting point of the reverse process, enabling the model to skip early denoising steps while preserving low-frequency structural consistency (see Figure 3 (c)). However, as shown in Figure 5 , this strategy suffers from two key limitations: (1) Local semantic repetition due to limited structural constraint. Since the structural prior is injected only at the initial stage, it is not maintained throughout the reverse process, causing the global semantic layout to gradually drift and often resulting in repetitive structures. (2) Details blurred due to low-frequency trajectory. Eq. 9 defines a transition trajectory starting from a blurred image, where x 0 , u ​ p H x_{0,up}^{H} lacks high-frequency components, and progressively evolves into Gaussian noise. As high-frequency information is absent throughout this trajectory, the reverse process tends to reconstructing predominantly low-frequency content, resulting in clean yet over-smoothed outputs with missing fine-grained details.

sections.text: To overcome these issues, we further impose structural and detail guidance during inference. Specifically, we aim to obtain a new velocity field v ^ θ H ​ ( t i ) \hat{v}^{\text{H}}_{\theta}(t_{i}) at each timestep t i t_{i} such that the inversion process (Eq. 4 ) ultimately generates high-resolution images x 0 H x^{H}_{0} with coherent structures and rich details. To guide the velocity refinement, we consider the single-step predicted clean image at time t i t_{i} : (10) x 0 ← t i H = x t i H + v t i H ​ ( 0 − t i ) x^{H}_{0\leftarrow t_{i}}=x^{H}_{t_{i}}+v^{H}_{t_{i}}(0-t_{i}) where x 0 ← t i H x^{H}_{0\leftarrow t_{i}} denotes the predicted clean image at time t i t_{i} with v t i H v^{H}_{t_{i}} fixed. To this end, we encourage each x 0 ← t i H x^{H}_{0\leftarrow t_{i}} to be structurally consistent and detail-rich, providing step-wise feedback to refine the velocity field throughout the entire inference trajectory. Since the velocity field governs the evolution trajectory toward x 0 x_{0} , improving these intermediate predictions leads to a more accurate and detail-preserving final result. Therefore, we investigate the variation of structural and detailed information across different resolutions and time steps t i t_{i} . As illustrated in Figure 6 , we make three key observations: (1) lower-resolution scales reduce repetitive patterns and produce more reasonable global semantic layouts; (2) higher-resolution scales generate richer details with sharper textures; and (3) as the denoising process progresses (i.e., as t i t_{i} decreases), fine-grained details gradually become clearer. Based on the above observations, we propose a structure–detail guidance strategy (SDG) to promote structural coherence while enhancing fine-grained details from two perspectives: cross-scale guidance and cross-temporal guidance . Figure 5 illustrates that, with the corrections from SDG, we are able to maintain coherent structural layouts while simultaneously improving the sharpness of fine-grained details.

sections.heading: 5. Experiments
sections.text: Experimental Settings. Following prior work ( Du et al., 2024b ; Bu et al., 2025 ) , we conduct experiments with Flux.1.0-dev ( Labs, 2024 ) at three resolutions: 2048 × \times 2048, 2048 × \times 4096, and 4096 × \times 4096. All experiments are implemented in PyTorch and run on an NVIDIA RTX 8000 GPU. Figure 7. Qualitative comparison with other methods on 2048 × 2048 2048\times 2048 and 2048 × 4096 2048\times 4096 . Red boxes highlight regions where our method produces clearer and more detailed results, while the blue box indicates dot-like artifacts generated by ScaleDiff. Zoom in for better visualization. Figure 8. Qualitative comparison with other methods on 4096 × 4096 4096\times 4096 . Red boxes highlight regions where our method produces clearer and more detailed results while yellow boxes mark the localized repetitive tiny structures produced by DemoFusion. Zoom in for better visualization. Evaluation. Following previous works ( Du et al., 2024a ; Qiu et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2025 ) , we collect 1K high-quality captions spanning diverse scenarios for image generation. For quantitative evaluation, we adopt widely used metrics including FID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) , KID ( Bińkowski et al., 2018 ) , and CLIP Score ( Radford et al., 2021 ) . FID and KID are computed between generated images and a reference set of 10K high-quality real images sourced from LAION-High-Resolution ( Schuhmann et al., 2022 ) . However, since FID and KID require resizing images to 299 × 299 299\times 299 , they may fail to capture fine-grained details in high-resolution generation, and thus often do not fully reflect perceptual quality ( Du et al., 2024a ; Jeong et al., 2025 ) . To address this limitation, following ( Kim et al., 2025 ; Qiu et al., 2024 ) , we compute FID and KID at the patch level, denoted as FID p and KID p , respectively, providing a more reliable assessment of high-resolution image quality.

sections.heading: 5.1. Comparison of Results
sections.text: High-resolution image generation methods can be broadly categorized into three groups: training-free diffusion models, super-resolution models, and training-based methods. In the main experiments, we primarily compare our method with training-free diffusion models, while super-resolution and training-based methods are evaluated in the ablation studies. For training-free diffusion models, we consider several state-of-the-art approaches, including three U-Net-based methods: (i) DemoFusion ( Du et al., 2024a ) , (ii) FreeScale ( Qiu et al., 2024 ) , and (iii) DiffuseHigh ( Kim et al., 2025 ) ; and three DiT-based methods: (iv) I-Max ( Du et al., 2024b ) , (v) ScaleDiff ( Koh et al., 2025 ) , and (vi) HiFlow ( Bu et al., 2025 ) . We first present qualitative comparisons of different methods in Figure 7 and Figure 8 , and make the following observations: (1) U-Net-based methods, such as DemoFusion, FreeScale, and DiffuseHigh, tend to produce structurally inconsistent results when generating ultra-high-resolution images. For example, at a resolution of 4096 × 4096 4096\times 4096 , these methods exhibit chaotic local structures in buildings. Moreover, DemoFusion is prone to local repetitive artifacts, such as duplicated small objects (e.g., multiple identical astronauts) at 2048 × 4096 2048\times 4096 . (2) Among the DiT-based methods, ScaleDiff tends to produce repetitive patterns, which are observed at both 2048 × 2048 2048\times 2048 and 2048 × 4096 2048\times 4096 . In addition, it occasionally introduces dot-like artifacts, as highlighted by the blue boxed region at 2048 × 4096 2048\times 4096 . In contrast, although I-Max and HiFlow do not exhibit such artifacts, their generated results tend to be overly smooth and lack fine details. Compared with these methods, our approach produces images with more coherent structural layouts and significantly richer details. Quantitative Comparison. We further present quantitative comparisons to evaluate the performance of different methods. As shown in Table 1 , we have the following observations: (1) On key visual quality metrics, including FID, KID, FID p , and KID p , our method consistently achieves the best performance across all evaluation settings, demonstrating its superior capability in generating high-quality high-resolution images. (2) For the image–text alignment metric (CLIP Score), our method achieves competitive performance, being only marginally lower than ScaleDiff under the 2048 × 4096 2048\times 4096 setting. Importantly, ScaleDiff is unable to perform inference at 4096 × 4096 4096\times 4096 due to GPU memory constraints, whereas our method remains stable and produces valid results at this resolution.

sections.text: Figure 10. Comparison of different attention mechanisms. Zoom in for better visualization. In this section, we evaluate TVSDA by comparing it with two alternative attention schemes: (1) the original joint self-attention (JSA) and (2) an overlapping patch-wise attention strategy (OPA) ( Bar-Tal et al., 2023 ) . Here, we only adopt the initial structural guidance (ISG) in all settings to maintain global structural coherence. Figure 10 compares different attention mechanisms. Both OPA and TVSDA improve fine-grained details over JSA. For example, in the bottom-right red box, JSA produces a blurry fence, whereas OPA and TVSDA generate sharper results. However, OPA operates on overlapping patches and requires smoothing fusion, introducing blurring artifacts. In contrast, TVSDA avoids patch overlap and yields clearer, more consistent details. For instance, background trees remain blurry with OPA, while our method produces sharper structures.

As the resolution increases, all methods incur higher computational costs. Nevertheless, our method consistently achieves the best efficiency across all settings. This speedup mainly comes from replacing global attention with local attention, which substantially reduces the attention computation, especially at high resolutions. Moreover, unlike ScaleDiff, our method remains stable at the highest resolution without out-of-memory issues, demonstrating better scalability for high-resolution image synthesis.

sections.heading: 6. Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we propose a training-free framework for high-resolution image generation with DiT models. Our method introduces text–visual scale-decoupled attention (TVSDA) to reduce semantic degradation by preserving global text perception while adapting image-token receptive fields to the training resolution. We further design structure–detail guidance (SDG), which improves structural coherence and fine details through cross-scale guidance (CSG) and cross-temporal guidance (CTG). Extensive experiments show that our method achieves better structure and detail fidelity than existing approaches.

Diffusion Transformer (DiT)-based text-to-image models have recently achieved remarkable success in image synthesis. However, when directly applied beyond their training resolution, these models often suffer from severe semantic degradation, where meaningful semantic content disappears. Although existing training-free high-resolution generation methods can mitigate this issue, the inherent semantic degradation at high resolutions remains largely unresolved, leading to degraded fine-grained details. Furthermore, widely used structural guidance methods lack modeling of the structure and details in the intermediate trajectory, which degrades the quality of the generated results. In this paper, we propose a training-free framework for high-resolution image generation to address these challenges. First, we propose a text–visual scale-decoupled attention (TVSDA) module, which restores the model’s ability to generate semantically meaningful content at high resolutions by preserving the global receptive field of text tokens while aligning the receptive field of image tokens with the training resolution. Second, we propose a structure–detail guidance (SDG) strategy that explicitly models structural information and fine details through scale-wise and temporal-wise guidance, overcoming the limitations of conventional low-resolution guidance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly improves both structural coherence and detail fidelity over existing training-free DiT-based high-resolution generation approaches. Introduction In recent years, text-to-image generation models ( Labs, 2024 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) based on Diffusion Transformers (DiT) ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) have substantially advanced image synthesis with remarkable visual quality. However, when the target resolution exceeds the training resolution, these models often fail dramatically ( Du et al., 2024b ; Bu et al., 2025 ) : meaningful semantic content disappears, and the generated images may collapse into semantically unrecognizable patterns, as shown in Figure 1 . This phenomenon, which we refer to as semantic degradation , has become a major obstacle for high-resolution generation scenarios. Figure 1. Illustrations of semantic degradation. When performing high-resolution inference with FLUX ( Labs, 2024 ) (trained at 1024 × \times 1024 and tested at 4096 × \times 4096), semantic structures completely disappear. Zoom in for better visualization. A straightforward solution is to further fine-tune pre-trained models on high-resolution images ( Guo et al., 2024 ; Hoogeboom et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Ren et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) . However, this strategy is often impractical due to the high computational cost and the limited availability of large-scale high-resolution training data. As a result, training-free high-resolution generation has attracted increasing attention ( He et al., 2024 ; Du et al., 2024a ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Bar-Tal et al., 2023 ; Lee et al., 2023 ; Du et al., 2024b ; Bu et al., 2025 ) . Early approaches were mainly developed for U-Net architectures ( He et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2024 ) , and are not readily applicable to DiT-based models. More recent studies ( Du et al., 2024b ; Bu et al., 2025 ) have begun to explore training-free high-resolution inference for DiTs, significantly improving generation quality. Despite recent progress, existing methods ( Du et al., 2024b ; Bu et al., 2025 ) primarily rely on low-resolution structural guidance, introducing structural priors during high-resolution inference rather than directly addressing the model’s intrinsic semantic degradation. If the model lacks the ability to generate semantically consistent content, such external guidance alone is insufficient to produce fine-grained details, as shown in Figure 2 . To address this issue, we propose a text-visual scale-decoupled attention (TVSDA) module to alleviate the model’s intrinsic semantic degradation at high resolutions. The core idea is to align the attention scale at high resolutions with that used during training. Concretely, attention for text tokens, which lack explicit positional information, is computed in a global manner, whereas attention for visual tokens with explicit positional information is confined within the training resolution. However, restoring semantic fidelity alone is not sufficient. Although TVSDA enables the model to generate semantically meaningful content, the resulting images often suffer from disorganized global layouts, manifested as repetitive local structures (see Figure 3 ). A natural next step is therefore to introduce a coarse structural prior, as in existing methods ( Du et al., 2024a ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Qiu et al., 2024 ; Bu et al., 2025 ) , to improve the global layout. Nevertheless, it still leaves two important residual failures (see Figure 5 ): (1) local semantic repetition, and (2) blurred fine details. These observations suggest that the remaining errors are no longer caused simply by a missing initial structure, but by a mismatch in how the reverse flow trajectory evolves at high resolution. This leads to the important question of our work: how should the high-resolution flow trajectory be corrected once semantic fidelity has been restored and a coarse structure has been initialized? To answer this, we perform an empirical analysis of the single-step predicted clean images across both different resolutions and different denoising timesteps (see Figure 6 ). We observe that lower-resolution predictions tend to provide more stable global semantic layouts, whereas higher-resolution predictions contain richer high-frequency details. Moreover, as denoising proceeds, later predictions become progressively sharper and reveal increasingly clear fine details. These observations suggest that structural coherence and fine-detail restoration should be guided in two ways: across scales and across timesteps. Based on this analysis, we propose a structure–detail guidance (SDG) strategy to refine the velocity field throughout inference. SDG consists of two key components. The first is Cross-Scale Guidance (CSG), which encourages the low-frequency components of the current high-resolution prediction to align with the structurally stable low-resolution prediction, while preserving the high-frequency components from the high-resolution branch. The second is Cross-Temporal Guidance (CTG), which leverages the progressive emergence of high-frequency details along the denoising trajectory to further sharpen fine structures. Ultimately, as shown in Figure 2 , with the integration of TVSDA and SDG, our method not only preserves coherent semantic layouts but also significantly enhances fine-grained details compared to previous methods. Figure 2. Visual comparison at 4096 × \times 4096 resolution. The contributions of this paper are summarized as follows. • We propose a text–visual scale-decoupled attention (TVSDA) module to restore semantic fidelity by preserving global text interactions while constraining visual attention to training local regions. • We show that conventional low-resolution structural guidance is a natural but insufficient remedy: although it improves coarse layout, it still leaves local semantic repetition and blurred details. To address these residual failures, we analyze predicted clean images across scales and timesteps, and derive a structure–detail guidance strategy consisting of Cross-Scale Guidance (CSG) and Cross-Temporal Guidance (CTG) to refine the high-resolution flow trajectory. • Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms prior training-free DiT-based approaches in both generation quality and inference efficiency on high-resolution image generation tasks. 2. Related Work 2.1. Text-to-Image Generation Diffusion models ( Blattmann et al., 2023 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Song et al., 2020 ) have emerged as the prevailing framework for text-to-image generation ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Podell et al., 2023 ) , owing to their strong capability in modeling complex high-dimensional distributions. Early works ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Ho and Salimans, 2022 ; Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) performed denoising at the pixel level, resulting in significantly high computational costs during both training and inference. The Latent Diffusion Model (LDM) ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) was subsequently introduced to mitigate these costs, enabling more efficient training and inference while enhancing the model’s ability to generate high-resolution images. Despite these advances, the training resolution of current diffusion models remains well below that required for many real-world applications. When the target resolution exceeds the training resolution, generation quality deteriorates substantially. Fine-tuning with high-resolution images ( Ren et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) can address this issue, but it is computationally expensive and limited by the availability of high-resolution data. 2.2. Training-Free High-Resolution Image Generation To address these issues, several works ( He et al., 2024 ; Du et al., 2024a ; Lee et al., 2023 ; Du et al., 2024b ; Bu et al., 2025 ) explore strategies to leverage pre-trained U-Net-based models (e.g., SDXL ( Podell et al., 2023 ) ) for high-resolution image generation without additional training. These methods can be broadly categorized into three types: (1) patch-wise methods ( Bar-Tal et al., 2023 ; Lee et al., 2023 ) , which divide the input into overlapping patches, perform standard denoising on each patch, and then fuse the results; (2) model component optimization methods ( He et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Jin et al., 2023 ) , which adapt selected components of the pre-trained model—such as self-attention layers ( Jin et al., 2023 ) or convolutional layers with dilated convolutions ( He et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2024 ) —for high-resolution generation; and (3) structural guidance methods ( Du et al., 2024a ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Qiu et al., 2024 ) , which leverage low-resolution images to provide semantic guidance for high-resolution generation. Recently, transformer-based diffusion models ( Labs, 2024 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) have significantly outperformed U-Net–based architectures. Consequently, several training-free high-resolution generation methods ( Du et al., 2024b ; Bu et al., 2025 ; Koh et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ; Yu et al., 2026 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) built on the transformer architecture have been proposed, which improve generation quality. However, these methods still tend to produce blurry results. In this work, we focus on high-resolution image generation using the transformer architecture. Unlike previous approaches, our method enhances generation quality by combining two strategies: restoring the model’s generative capabilities and refining the reverse denoising trajectory with structural and detail guidance. 3. Text-Visual Scale-Decoupled Attention In the joint self-attention layer, as the resolution increases, the receptive field of each query token grows quadratically ( Jin et al., 2023 ) , making attention overly uniform at high resolutions, causing it to attend to many irrelevant regions, and ultimately leading to semantic degradation. To mitigate this issue, we aim to align attention computation with the training resolution during high-resolution generation. For a visual query token q v i q_{\mathrm{v}}^{i} , which is associated with an explicit spatial position, it is natural to constrain its receptive field to the local region centered on itself, with a scale consistent with the training resolution. In contrast, a text query token q t i q_{\mathrm{t}}^{i} , lacking explicit positional priors, is not constrained in the same way. Motivated by this, we propose a text-visual scale-decoupled attention mechanism (TVSDA), which decouples attention scales for text and visual tokens.
